NODE VERSION DRIFT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Do your package.json, .nvmrc, Dockerfile and CI agree on which Node.js to run?

Paste the files that declare a Node.js version and see where they drift apart: a pinned version that cannot satisfy engines.node, pins that disagree on the major version across files, a CI matrix or pin on an end-of-life Node.js, and an engines.node range with no upper bound and nothing pinned.

Nothing is uploaded. Everything runs in this browser against the text you paste in. End-of-life dates are a static table copied from nodejs.org on 2026-10-11 and shown as of the date you pick.

Check a repo's Node.js versions

Leave a box empty if the repo has no such file. The boxes start with a worked example that has real drift in it.

    Prefer a CLI, or want this in CI before a merge?

    Same logic, zero dependencies, one command per repo:

    node cli.mjs                       # scan the current directory
node cli.mjs /path/to/repo         # scan a specific checkout
node cli.mjs --format json
node cli.mjs --fail-on-risk        # exit 2 if any risk finding exists
node cli.mjs --today 2026-10-11    # judge end-of-life as of a fixed date

    Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node.js 18+, nothing to install, no network call ever. --fail-on-risk makes it a one-line CI gate.

    What's checked

    CheckHow
    Pin violates engines.nodeA version from .nvmrc, .node-version, .tool-versions, a Dockerfile FROM node: tag, Volta's volta.node or a setup-node step that no matching version could satisfy against engines.node
    Majors disagreeNon-matrix pins in different files that name different Node.js majors (a CI matrix is meant to test several, so it is exempt)
    End-of-life Node.jsAny pin or matrix entry whose major is past its end-of-life date in the dated table, plus a notice when one is within 90 days
    Unbounded enginesengines.node like >=18 with no upper bound while no file pins a Node.js version at all

    Aliases such as lts/*, latest and node change over time, so they are listed as notices and never guessed. A ${{ matrix.x }} reference is resolved from the workflow's own matrix. Also read: why Node.js versions drift, and how this compares to eyeballing the files or npm's engine-strict.

    Common questions

    Why check Node.js versions across files at all?

    A repo usually states its Node.js version in four or five places that nobody keeps in step: engines.node in package.json, an .nvmrc, the Dockerfile base image, and the GitHub Actions setup-node step. When they drift, local development, CI and production quietly run different majors, so a bug appears in one and not the others, or a dependency that needs a newer Node.js is installed on an older one.

    How does it decide whether a pin satisfies engines.node?

    It has its own small semver range parser (caret, tilde, comparators, hyphen ranges, x-ranges, spaces as AND, double pipe as OR). A pin such as 20 is treated as any 20.x version, so it is only flagged when no 20.x version could possibly satisfy the range; an exact pin such as 20.4.0 is checked exactly.

    Where do the end-of-life dates come from, and can they go stale?

    They come from a small table copied from the Node.js release schedule at nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases, labelled with the date it was written. Even majors end on April 30 of their third year and odd majors are never long-term support. The table is a snapshot, so a major newer than the table is reported as unknown rather than supported, and you should confirm anything important on nodejs.org.

    Is anything uploaded?

    No. Everything is computed in your browser from the text you paste in, and nothing you type is sent anywhere. The CLI makes no network call either; it only reads files already on your own disk.

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not engineering advice, and it does not replace running your tests on the Node.js version you actually deploy. The end-of-life dates come from a static table copied from nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases on 2026-10-11 and may be out of date; check nodejs.org for the current schedule. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

    Everything runs in your browser. Nothing you type is ever uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (versions_checked, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

vs-eyeballing-and-npm-engine-strict.html.text:
← Back to the checker

This checker vs. eyeballing the files and npm's engine-strict

There are three ordinary ways to keep a repo's Node.js versions honest: read the files yourself during review, turn on engine-strict so an install under the wrong runtime fails, and look at what npm ls reports. Each answers a real question. None of them compares your Dockerfile, your workflow and your .nvmrc to each other, which is the question this checker is for.

What each one is for

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is the Node.js running this install inside engines.node?engine-strict (an npm configuration setting). It checks the runtime doing the install, and nothing else.
Do my installed dependencies declare an engines field this runtime does not meet?npm ls and the install warnings. This checker does not read node_modules at all.
Can the Node.js my Dockerfile or CI uses ever satisfy engines.node?This checker. The runtime never meets the range until something runs under it.
Do .nvmrc, the Dockerfile and CI name the same major?This checker, or a careful read of every file.
Is anything pinned past its end-of-life date?This checker, against a dated table. Reading the files tells you the number, not whether it is still supported.
Is anything uploaded?Neither. This checker runs in your browser or reads local files only.

Common questions

Doesn't npm already warn when my Node.js version is outside engines?

Only for the Node.js that is running the install, and only as a warning unless engine-strict is turned on. It never looks at the version your Dockerfile or CI workflow will use, so a pin that can never satisfy engines.node is invisible until someone happens to run an install under that exact runtime.

What does npm ls tell me about Node.js versions?

It lists the dependency tree installed in node_modules, and it can report packages whose own engines field does not match the running Node.js. It does not read .nvmrc, the Dockerfile or any workflow file, and it cannot tell you that two of your own files name different majors.

When is eyeballing the files good enough?

For a small repo where all the versions sit in one or two files, reading them takes seconds and is perfectly adequate. It stops being reliable with a monorepo, several Dockerfiles, a workflow matrix that references matrix.node, and a range such as ^20.5 || >=22 that you have to evaluate in your head against a bare 20.

Do I have to choose one?

No. Keep engine-strict if you want installs to fail on an unsupported runtime, and keep reading the files in review. This tool covers the part neither does, which is comparing every declared version to every other one, and to a dated end-of-life table, in a single pass.

No warranty. This page and the linked checker is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not engineering advice, and it does not replace running your tests on the Node.js version you actually deploy. The end-of-life dates come from a static table copied from nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases on 2026-10-11 and may be out of date; check nodejs.org for the current schedule. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Descriptions of engine-strict and npm ls are based on npm's public documentation at docs.npmjs.com and are summarised, not quoted; check it for exact current behaviour. This page says "different job", not "better": npm's own checks remain the right tool for what they check.

why-node-version-drift-happens.html.text:
← Back to Node Version Drift Check

Why Node.js versions drift between package.json, .nvmrc, Docker and CI

A Node.js project states which runtime it wants in up to five places: engines.node in package.json, an .nvmrc or .node-version file, an asdf .tool-versions line, the FROM node: line of a Dockerfile, and the node-version of a GitHub Actions actions/setup-node step (Volta users add volta.node). Each is read by a different tool. None of those tools reads the others.

The four kinds of drift

FindingExampleWhat goes wrong
Pin violates engines.nodeengines.node is >=22, .nvmrc says 20.11.1Local development runs a Node.js your own package says it does not support; installs warn, or fail where engine-strict is on.
Majors disagreeDockerfile on node:22, CI on node-version: 20Tests pass on one major and production runs another.
End-of-life Node.jsA CI matrix still lists 18The line no longer receives security fixes, and you are testing a version you should not be shipping.
Unbounded engines>=18 and no pin anywhereNo file records which version was ever tested.

Reading the end-of-life table

The dates come from the Node.js release schedule at nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases: 18 ended 2025-04-30, 20 ended 2026-04-30, 22 ends 2027-04-30 and 24 ends 2028-04-30. Odd majors are never long-term support and end about six months after release. The table inside the tool is dated 2026-10-11 and is only a snapshot, which is why every finding says "per the table dated" and why --today exists: it makes the verdict reproducible in a test.

Run it in CI

node cli.mjs --fail-on-risk

Exit status 2 means at least one risk finding. Notices (aliases the tool will not guess at, an engines range that still admits an end-of-life major, a major that ends within 90 days) are printed but do not fail the run.

Common questions

Why do Node.js versions in a repo drift apart?

Each file is edited for a different reason by a different person. Someone bumps the Dockerfile for a security fix, someone else raises engines.node when a dependency needs it, and the .nvmrc and the CI workflow are only touched when something breaks. Nothing in npm, Docker or GitHub Actions compares them to each other, so the disagreement lasts until a bug makes it visible.

What does an unbounded engines.node range actually risk?

A range like >=18 says every future major will do. It will happily install on a Node.js version released next year that none of your dependencies or tests have ever run on, and with nothing pinned in .nvmrc, the Dockerfile or CI there is no file that says which version you actually tested. A bounded range such as >=22 <25, or a pin, records the versions you stand behind.

Why are odd-numbered Node.js versions treated differently?

Odd-numbered releases never enter long-term support and stop receiving fixes roughly six months after release, so the table marks their dates as approximate. Even-numbered releases become long-term support and are maintained until April 30 of their third calendar year. A pin on an odd major in a Dockerfile or CI is therefore usually a leftover rather than a decision.

What does this checker deliberately not do?

It does not run Node.js, install packages, or ask any registry which versions exist. It cannot tell you what lts/* or latest mean today, so those are listed as notices. It treats prerelease tags as their release, only reads the first nodejs line of a .tool-versions file, and judges end-of-life from a static table that you should confirm against nodejs.org before acting on a finding.
